title: This Owl Lives in a Hole and Hisses Like a Rattlesnake

scenes.text: There's a rattlesnake in this burrow. Except it's a bird.
The burrowing owl barely digs. It moves into empty prairie dog holes and raises its chicks underground.
Rattlesnakes use the same holes. So when something pokes its nose into the burrow, the owl lets out a long, rattling hiss.
In 1986, scientists played that hiss to ground squirrels. The squirrels were almost as alarmed as when they heard a real rattlesnake.
The sound likely evolved to copy a cornered rattlesnake's warning. Most visitors don't stay to check.
Scientists call it acoustic mimicry. The owl calls it home security. So, who's in the hole?

description:
The burrowing owl nests in abandoned rodent burrows, often prairie dog holes, and when cornered it gives a long rattling hiss that mimics a rattlesnake.
In a 1986 study by Matthew Rowe and colleagues (Ethology), California ground squirrels reacted to the owl's hiss almost as strongly as to a recording of a real rattlesnake; the call is considered one of the first confirmed cases of acoustic defensive mimicry.
What other animal pretends to be something more dangerous?
subject: burrowing owl
first_comment: Mice and big insects are its main food, hunted from a hole a few inches wide on legs that look far too long for an owl. Which bird would you put at number one for cleverness?
